articles.text: It now seems settled that Govenor Pierce will serve out his term of office. Ziebach has been appointed receiver of public monies at Yankton and as there is no other opposition to our present governor, his tenure of office will likely remain undisturbed.
articles.summary: With Ziebach appointed receiver at Yankton, Governor Pierce appears secure to serve out his term.

articles.text: We are in receipt of a letter from Lieut. J. M. T. Partello, dated at Anvers, Belgium, in which he states that he and his wife are having glorious times. They are "doing" Europe in good shape and we hope at some time to publish one of his interesting descriptions of travel. He is as fine a writer as he is a marksman.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy received a letter from Lieut. J. M. T. Partello, touring Europe with his wife.

articles.text: Mandan is not the only place that is troubled with itinerant insurance men. Some of the snide fellows have been to Medora, trying to work the honest citizens at that place. Editor Packard, who is the agent doing business there with honest companies on honest basis, is justly indignant. He may tell his patrons and readers that the experience of Mandan people with these travelling agents is bad. They are a lot of dishonest scoundrels.—[Mandan Pioneer.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Mandan Pioneer warning against itinerant insurance agents who had been working Medora, where Packard is the insurance agent.

articles.text: The government astronomers and surveyors operating on the line between Dakota and Montana have completed their labor. The length of the east line of Montana is 277 miles geographical survey. These officials chained it making it 276 miles 27 chains and 80 links, which is good chaining. The line crosses the railroad about 6½ miles east of Mingusville and leaves Ayott's ranch about four miles in Montana. The survey is now definitely settled and the line clearly defined.—[Glendive Times.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Glendive Times: the Dakota-Montana boundary survey is complete, crossing the railroad about 6½ miles east of Mingusville.

articles.text: The COW BOY subscribers for this year and next year will get more than they bargained for. There will be fifty-three issues each year. An interesting case will soon be tried, in which the editor of an eastern weekly published on Thursday is sued by a subscriber, because the editor skipped an issue. The subscriber claims that he was to receive the paper every week and the editor claims that he was to furnish only as many copies of his paper as there are weeks in the year, fifty-two. Pending the decision of this suit and barring accidents, the COW BOY will appear every Thursday and throw in the extra issues to its subscribers.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy says it will publish all fifty-three Thursday issues this year and next.

articles.text: Nothing definite has been learned concerning the organization of the county. No steps have been taken in Bismarck to carry out the plan of organization on account of the protest offered by F. B. Allen. It seems scarcely credible that the wishes of 174 citizens can be so long thwarted, but the end must soon come. The governor is perfectly right in taking time to consider the matter and he cannot but become satisfied soon that the people of Billings county want the county organized. Only two refusals of voters to sign and 174 legal signatures is an overwhlming majority that is rarely duplicated. The foundation principle of our Democratic form of government will be overthrown, if this or any other majority is not allowed to rule.
articles.summary: Billings county organization remains stalled at Bismarck because of F. B. Allen's protest, despite a petition with 174 signatures.

articles.text: We are in receipt of Governor Pierce's annual message to the Secretary of the Interior. It is published in the form of a large, fifty-three-page pamphlet and contains information extremely valuable to anyone wishing to learn about Dakota. From this report, it appears that we had at the last census, 416,000 population and this number is increasing at the rate of sixty-six per cent. per annum. In 1880 there were 17,435 farms in the territory and in 1885 there were 82,017. Banks increased from twenty-four in 1880 to 195 in 1885, with capitals of $440,000 and $4,514,000 respectively. The total number of miles of rail-road now in operation in Dakota, is 2,701. Although Dakota is not rated at all as a manufacturisg territory she has $6,593,218 invested in manufacturing industries, exclusive of the mining industries of the Black Hills. The total bonded debt of the territory is $568,2000, which will be or has by this time been increased $176,000, authorized at the last session of the legislature and bringing 103.2. The report ends with a number of tables, from which we glean the fol- figures on Billings county: We have a population of 737, of whom 518 are males. It appears that we have about as small an area of land under cultivation as any county, the total acreage being 167. We have, however more cattle than any county in the territory except Fall River, the total value being $1,226,380.
articles.summary: Summary of Governor Pierce's annual report on Dakota, including Billings county figures: population 737, 167 acres cultivated, cattle worth $1,226,380.

articles.headline: As Others See It.
articles.text:
The so-called government of the southern half of that territory is a mere make-believe. The so-called legislative assembly at Huron is a hollow and tasteless sham. The so-called senators that have been appointed by that hollow sham are a couple of private citizens that are not senators in any meaning or suggestion of that word. The so-called governor at Huron is a person who is playing governor. The so-called legislature is an assembly of persons that are playing legislature. Huron is a youthful and ambitious town that presents the novel attraction of a new kind of theater comique, where a company of Dakota politicians are performing an original farce for the edification of a more or less fashionable audience. The part that each represents is that of Bottom the Weaver enacting the lion. They are roaring the same as if they were real lions, instead of absurd Bottoms.

There is not a grain, a color, a shadow, a tint, or even a faint tinge of authority for the existence of the company of political comedians at Huron, or that casts a reflection of the faintest validity on anything they have done, are doing, or may do. The pair of pretended senators they have appointed will not occupy any seats in the senate; the pretended statutes they have enacted will not be laws nor have the slightest effect of law; the expenses they are incurring will create no form or likeness of any public obligation to pay, and will be paid honestly only by the individual performers that incur them. The southern half of Dakota will not be politically organized by the name of "[stuff?]." The scheme of cutting Dakota in twain to make more offices for the political immigrants and more taxation for the struggling pioneers that are not seeking offices, is a speculative scheme of wrong that ought not to be executed, and will not be executed. The company of political comedians that are playing government at Huron would do well, therefore, to close the dramatic season and retire to attend their own business, if they have any.—[Chicago Times.
articles.summary: Chicago Times piece reprinted by the Cow Boy ridiculing the South Dakota statehood government at Huron.

articles.text: Vol. 1, No. 1, of the North Dakota Farmer, published at Jamestown, is at hand. Typographically and editorially it is as near perfection as any agricultural paper we have seen. If it "keeps up its lick," it will be a credit to Dakota journalism and set a mark for agricultural papers of the east to copy after.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy praises the first issue of the North Dakota Farmer of Jamestown.

articles.text: The article clipped from the Glendive Times, relative to the Dakota-Montana line is of especial interest to the people of our county. All persons living east of a line drawn north and south six and one-half miles east of Mingusville, are in Billings county, Dakota. It will be comparatively easy for all to decide where they are located. Probably, also, the line is marked in such a way that it will be an easy matter for those located near it to tell in which territory they are.
articles.summary: Comment that everyone east of a line 6½ miles east of Mingusville lives in Billings county, Dakota.

articles.text: In considering the beef market as a basis from which to figure on the future, do not forget that many thousands of cattle, especially from Texas and the Cherokee strip, have been thrown upon the market this year that were not fit for market and would never have been sold for beef but for circumstances well known and over which the owners had no control. While this heavy run of inferior cattle has to an extent paralyzed the market, it has at the same time diminished the supply.—[Texas Stockman.
articles.summary: Texas Stockman reprint on how forced sales of inferior Texas and Cherokee strip cattle depressed the market but cut supply.

articles.text: The wild horses of Wyoming and Western Nebraska are compact little animals weighing from 800 to 1,100 pounds. The majority of them stand 14 hands high. In color they are usually brown, sorrel or bay. A gray is seldom seen, unless it has strayed away from civilization. Their tails grow long frequently dragging on the ground, but their manes are like those of other horses and not growing to the knees as are represented in some books. The eye, probably from being constantly on the watch, is larger than the eye of the domestic horse, and even when tamed the eye remains a distinctive mark of the horse's origin. Wild horses when captured or tamed are superior to other horses of the same size. Many of them are used by the cow boys and others are broken to harness and driven as carriage horses, being entirely trustworthy.—[Hoof & Horn.
articles.summary: Hoof & Horn reprint describing the wild horses of Wyoming and western Nebraska.

articles.headline: Estrays—Laws of Dakota.
articles.text:
Estrays can only be taken up by house holders, claim holders, under United States land laws, and then only when such estray is found in the immediate vicinity of his or her claim or place of residence in the county wherein he or she resides, except that any person may, when the estray is found ten miles from any habitation, in an uninhabited part of the territory.

Estrays cannot be taken up between the first day of October and March 1, inclusive, unless found trespassing upon the premises or within the enclosure of the person taking the same up.

Publishing notice—Whenever any person shall take up an estray, he or they must, within fifteen days thereafter, give notice of such taking up or finding three times in a weekly newspaper printed in the county wherein such estray is taken up.

If such estray be not claimed or called for within twenty-two days after the first insertion of such notice in a newspaper, such taker up or finder must go before a justice of the peace of the county wherein he resides and make oath to the facts in the case.

A warrant [must then be?] issued by the justice to three (3) householders of the county to appraise such estray, and report marks, brands, description valuation and name and place of residence of taker to such justice in writing, under oath.

Publication by justice—Whereupon the justice must immediately publish such report and appraisment according to law.

Register of deeds must keep a book entitled "Estray Register," and record such reports therein.

Upon claim being made to the ownership of such estray, both the taker up or finder and claimant shall go before the justice, and the claimant make oath to his name, place of residence, ownership and description of property, after which, upon payment of all fees advanced by him and reasonable charges, such estray must be delivered up.

At the expiration of one year after such taking up or finding, if the taker up or finder has caused the same to have been advertised and appraised, and is not to exceed in value fifty dollars, title shall rest in taker up or finder.

If over the value of fifty dollars, notice must be given to such justice of the peace or his successor; such justice shall then appoint a day of sale, and cause the same to be published three (3) times in a weekly newspaper published within the county, fixing a day of sale at the county seat, sale to be made by the justice; and after paying from the proceeds of the sale the cost of advertisements and all legal costs and charges, pay to the county treasurer the residue of the proceeds, and take his receipt therefor.

If the moneys so deposited be not claimed within six months therafter, and proper proof made, the same shall be by the county treasurer paid to the school fund.

The justice must also file with the treasurer a certificate setting forth a description of the estray, marks and brands and name of taker up.

The fees of the justice—advertising and appraising must be paid by the taker up or finder and be a first lien thereon.

Any person not authorized, taking up an estray, failing to advertise the same, imprudently working or failing to properly feed the same, shall forfeit to the owner the sum of $25, and be recovered by action for debt before any justice of the peace. The taker up may work the estray in a prudent manner.

Should any estray, after being taken up and advertised, be lost or injure without negligence on the part of the taker up, he is not liable to the owner.—[N. W. Farmer.
articles.summary: Summary of Dakota territorial law on taking up and advertising estray livestock, reprinted from the N. W. Farmer.

articles.text: The school is in flourishing condition, and praises of Mr. Simmers' instruction are numerous. There are now twenty-six scholars in attendance. A night school is conductec in addition.

articles.text: James Hannigan returned from Bismarck Tuesday evening. The Tribune speaks of him as "a distinguished Frenchman from Medora." It won't do, Monsieur de Quinn, Jim. is no countryman of yours.
articles.summary: James Hannigan returned from Bismarck; the Cow Boy jokes about the Tribune calling him a Frenchman.

articles.text: Even for Dakota, this weather is wonderful. So far this fall we have not had ten days of anything resembling winter weather. To-day is a perfect fall day. The sun is shining brightly, the thermometer registers 41 in the shade and in the sunshine it is if anything, too warm. We feel for the denizens of the frozen-up States.
articles.summary: Unusually mild weather: 41 degrees in the shade on the issue day.

articles.text: A large variety of Holiday meats can be found at Willard & Keeler's meat market. articles.text: A remark, expressive of surprise was made last week, at our ability to turn out a certain kind of job work. Lest others should have the same idea, we "wish to remark" that we have abundant facilities for turning out almost any kind of job work and guarantee our work in every case, equal to the same class of work done anywhere.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy advertises its job-printing capacity.

articles.text: We do not believe much in the practice some papers adopt, of offering premiums to gain subscribers, but as the COW BOY will be a three-year-old soon we wish to have a number of new subscribers to add to our already large and growing list. To this end, between now and March 1, we will send the paper for a year from next March for the regular rate of $2. In addition, we will give the person bringing us the greatest number of new subscribers, $10 in cash. In all cases, as heretofore, subscriptions must be accompanied with the cash. This offer ceases and the prize will be awarded on March 1. A little effort is likely to win the prize and the combined efforts of a number of our friends will make a gratifying increase in our list.
articles.summary: Subscription offer and a $10 prize for bringing in the most new subscribers by March 1.

articles.text: Mr. Ba-a-d Man Finnegan again put himself on exhibition last Sunday. After filling up with "valley-tan" he tried some of his "Bad man from Bitter creek" idiocy and came near doing some fatal work with his rifle, before Fred Willard relieved him of it. He was taken to Dickinson Monday morning by Sheriff Sebastian and pleading guilty to the charge of discharging fire-arms in a public place, was given a Christmas present of $5 and costs by Justice Starr, which will net him about twenty days in jail. We have heard several apologists for Finnegan say that he would not have done as he did if he had been sober. This is no argument, either in law or the commonest of common sense. He has repeatedly done the same thing previously and it is high time that he was made to feel that there can be some control over him. Mr. Willard did his duty both as a citizen and an officer in putting a quietus on Mr. B. M. Finnegan.
articles.summary: Drunken Finnegan nearly shot someone, was disarmed by Fred Willard, and was fined $5 and costs at Dickinson.
